relationships.description: An oauth2-type security scheme contains the OAuth flows object that declares which grant types clients may use to obtain tokens under that scheme, and the flows object has no meaning outside it.
relationships.evidence: In the OpenAPI document, the scheme under components.securitySchemes has type: oauth2 and a nested flows object listing grant types such as authorizationCode or clientCredentials.

relationships.description: The security scheme is the concrete API-level credential mechanism that puts into effect the authentication part of an access-control policy, for example a policy requiring bearer tokens on all endpoints.
relationships.evidence: The security policy document or policy-as-code file names the required authentication mechanism, and the API description declares a matching scheme that the protected operations reference in their security requirements.

relationships.description: Credentials presented under the security scheme identify a particular principal, so the scheme corresponds to the actor population (human users, service accounts, or partners) it authenticates.
relationships.evidence: Authentication middleware or identity-provider configuration resolves tokens or API keys issued for the scheme to a specific user pool, client registration, or service account.

relationships.description: The credentials or sessions the security scheme validates are held in a persistent store, such as an API-key table, an OAuth client table, or a session bucket, that is checked when a request is verified.
relationships.evidence: The key-validation or token-introspection code for the scheme queries a named table, collection, or key-value bucket that holds API keys, client secrets, or sessions.

relationships.description: The security scheme points to the application component that issues or validates its credentials, such as an authorization server, identity service, or authentication gateway module.
relationships.evidence: The scheme's tokenUrl, authorizationUrl, or openIdConnectUrl resolves to an endpoint hosted by that component, or the component's authentication handler is registered under the scheme's name.

relationships.description: The security scheme points to the application service, such as a token-issuance or identity-verification service, whose operations clients call to obtain or validate the credentials the scheme expects.
relationships.evidence: The scheme's OAuth or OpenID Connect URLs or its x- extension metadata name operations of the token or identity service listed in the service catalog.

relationships.description: The security scheme points to the business channel, such as a partner portal or customer self-service portal, through which clients are onboarded and receive the credentials the scheme requires.
relationships.evidence: The scheme description or the developer documentation tells clients to register or request API keys through a named portal or channel.

relationships.description: The security scheme points to the business service, such as partner onboarding or customer account access, that it controls access to or that issues the clients' credentials.
relationships.evidence: The scheme description, an x- extension, or an architecture traceability record links the scheme to the named business service it gates or supports.

relationships.description: The security scheme points to a protected resource in the access-control model that callers authenticated through it may try to reach.
relationships.evidence: The operations that carry the scheme in their security requirements expose paths that the security model registers as secure resources, or the access-control configuration names the scheme for that resource.

relationships.description: Using the security scheme to reach protected operations depends on callers holding specific permissions, typically expressed as OAuth scopes the scheme declares and that map to permission grants.
relationships.evidence: The OAuth flows' scopes map, or the scopes listed in operation security requirements, correspond one-to-one with permission identifiers defined in the authorization model or checked by enforcement middleware.

relationships.description: The choice and configuration of the security scheme conform to an architectural principle, such as 'use standard token-based authentication' or 'zero trust for all APIs'.
relationships.evidence: An architecture decision record or design review cites the principle as the rationale for adopting the scheme type, for example OpenID Connect over custom API keys.

relationships.description: The security scheme meets a specific, verifiable authentication requirement, such as 'all partner APIs shall require OAuth 2.0 client credentials'.
relationships.evidence: A requirements traceability matrix or a security test links the requirement ID to the scheme, and the test confirms that unauthenticated calls to operations using the scheme are rejected.

relationships.description: The security scheme provides the means by which people or systems in a business role, such as a partner integrator or customer, prove their identity to use the API.
relationships.evidence: Identity-provider configuration or API onboarding documentation issues credentials for the scheme to principals assigned to that role, for example a partner client registration per integrator.

relationships.description: The security scheme provides the authentication mechanism that an API operation relies on to verify callers before it handles a request.
relationships.evidence: The operation's security array, or the root-level security inherited by that operation, names the scheme, and the route handler is wrapped by the authentication middleware registered for it.

relationships.description: The security scheme depends on platform software, such as an identity server, API gateway, or key-value cache, to issue, store, or validate its credentials at runtime.
relationships.evidence: Deployment or gateway configuration, such as a Keycloak realm, an Envoy JWT filter, or a Redis session store, implements validation for the scheme's token or key type.

notes: The four references edges to application/business elements are vague; uses.systemsoftware likely overlaps references.applicationcomponent. maps-to targets (Actor, Collection) misuse a schema-mapping predicate; consider authenticates→Actor and accesses→Collection. implements SecurityPolicy overstates it, since a scheme covers authentication only; supports or enforces fits better. satisfies Principle conflicts with the Principle definition, which says it is not directly verifiable; governed-by-principles fits better.
